CHAPTER -I 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1 INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1.1 The North Eastern Region collectively represe nts eight States of the North East viz. 
Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizor am, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. The 
region possesses enormous potential and opportuniti es and also inherent challenges.  However, 
the challenges associated with development of the r egion and aspirations of people of these eight 
States require special attention due to following special features:- 
• The seven States of the North Eastern Region barrin g Sikkim are linked to the rest of 
India through  a narrow 26 km long Siliguri Corrido r commonly known as Chicken's 
neck.  They therefore form an integrated geographical unit. 
• 98% of NER's border is bounded by India's international neighbours. 
• The region offers great diversity – of topography, climatic conditions, language, religion, 
ethnicity and yet has common developmental challenges. 
• Most of the region is hilly and contains difficult terrain. 
• While Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram are overwhelmingly tribal, the 
other four States also have substantial tribal population. 
• Infrastructure deficit in the region, particularly connectivity in all forms is acute. 
• The economy of the region is overwhelmingly agricultural. 
For the above reasons, the Department of Developmen t of North Eastern Region was set up in 
September, 2001 under the Ministry of Home Affairs and subsequently upgraded to a full-fledged 
Ministry in May 2004 underscoring its complete comm itment to ensure development with equity 
for the NER to unleash the potential of its human and natural resources. 
 
1.2 MANDATE AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
1.2.1 Ministry of Development of North Eastern Regi on or DONER, as it is commonly known, 
is a unique Ministry in the Union Government as its  activities are regional and more importantly 
advocating the special needs of the region to the other Ministries/Departments and policy makers.  
The Ministry has been assigned matters relating to planning, execution and monitoring of 
development schemes and projects in North East Region.  

1.2.2 The Ministry of DONER funds projects through various schemes of NEC and also through 
other scheme namely, Non - Lapsable Central Pool of  Resources (NLCPR), to create socio-
economic infrastructure in the region.  The scheme inter-alia aims at filling critical gaps in existing 
developmental programmes/schemes.  Apart from infra structure development in the region, the 
Ministry also funds schemes of Advocacy & Publicity  for showcasing potential of North Eastern 
Region and that of Technical Assistance & Capacity Building for training youth of the region and 
State Government/Public Sector employees of the reg ion.  The Ministry has also started 
implementing Central Sector Plan Scheme titled NLCP R Central in 2012-13 to supplement efforts 
of central Ministries/Departments for development o f infrastructure in the region. The Ministry’s 
Plan allocation has steadily increased from Rs.1019 .90 crore in 2002-03 to Rs.2430.01  crore in 
2016-17.    
1.2.3 In order to help the region to optimize benef its of funding from Government of India, 
review meetings are being organized from time to ti me,   which are attended by senior 
functionaries of the State Governments and the conc erned Ministries/Departments of Government 
of India. Various policy and procedural decisions a re taken in these meetings.  In addition, the 
Ministry follows up mobilization of external aid fo r catalyzing development in the region through 
road construction, livelihood project, etc.  
1.2.4 There are two Central Public Sector Enterpris es (CPSEs) under administrative control of 
the Ministry, viz., North Eastern Handicrafts and H andloom Development Corporation Ltd., 
(NEHHDC) and North Eastern Regional Agricultural Ma rketing Corporation Ltd., (NERAMAC). 
The Objective of NEHHDC is development and procurem ent of handicrafts and handloom items 
from artisans and weavers of the region. The Mandat e of NERAMAC includes supporting 
farmers/producers of north east getting remunerativ e prices for their produce and thereby bridge 
the gap between the farmers and the market and also  enhancing the agricultural procurement, 
processing and marketing infrastructure of the Northeast Region of India. Government is supposed 
to extend Non-Plan assistance to both these Corporations. 
1.2.5 Ministry of DoNER also provides interest-free  loan to North Eastern Development 
Finance Corporation Ltd . (NEDFi) - a financial institution - which in turn  provides credit and 
other facilities to industrial enterprises, infrast ructure projects, agro-horticulture units etc. in N E 
region for promotion, expansion and modernisation.  It also provides microfinance in all eight 
states of NER. 
1.2.6 The Objectives of Ministry of DoNER revolve around the following:- 
 

i) Accelerating the pace of socio-economic development  in the North Eastern 
Region. 
ii) Synergizing the efforts of Central/State Government s/Other Stakeholders for 
balanced development of the Region. 
iii) Integrated & holistic planning for the Region, taki ng into account the heightened 
consciousness of the people of the Region, their as pirations, needs and 
sensitivities.  
iv) Evolving a common approach for all the agencies wor king for the development of 
the Region. 
v) Formulating appropriate policies for the rapid development of the Region. 
 
1.2.7 As per Allocation of Business Rules, Governme nt of India,  this Ministry is inter alia  
concerned with following: - 
• Matters relating to the planning, execution and mon itoring of developmental 
schemes and projects of North Eastern Region includ ing those in the sectors of 
Power, Irrigation, Roads and Communications. 
• Non-lapsable Fund for the North Eastern Region. 
• North Eastern Council (NEC) 
• North Eastern Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi) 
• North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corpo ration Limited 
(NERAMAC). 
• North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation (NEHHDC) 
• Road works financed in whole or in part by the Cent ral Government in the North 
Eastern Region. 
• Planning of Road and Inland Waterways Transport in the North Eastern Region. 
  
1.3 POLICY FRAMEWORK 
 
1.3.1 The Ministry implements work mandated in para  1.2.1 through formulations of 
appropriate policies, and implementation of specifi c Plan programmes.  North Eastern Council, 
Shillong also implements various Plan Schemes in the Region.   
 
1.3.2  All non-exempted Ministries/Departments of G overnment of India are required to 
earmark at least 10% of Gross Budgetary Support (GB S) towards development of North Eastern 
States for creation of both economic and social inf rastructure.  Since 1998-99, annual unspent 

amount out of outlays earmarked for NE Region by no n-exempted Central 
Ministries/Departments is being accounted as accrua l to Central Resource Pool  for Development 
of North Eastern Region which is maintained on prof orma basis by Ministry of Finance and is 
known as Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NL CPR).  Accruals from this Pool are 
utilized for financing new infrastructure projects/ schemes in the Region under NLCPR Plan 
Scheme implemented by Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region.  
 
1.3.3 The Ministry also supervises work of Public S ector Enterprises, North Eastern 
Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation L td. (NEHHDC) and North Eastern 
Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Ltd. (N ERAMAC).  The Government provides 
interest free loan to the North Eastern Development  Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi), a 
financial institution which, inter alia provides cr edit and other facilities to industrial enterprises , 
infrastructure projects, agro-horticulture units et c.  in the Region for promotion, expansion and 
modernisation.    
 
1.3.4 While respective Ministries/Departments are r esponsible in respect of subjects allocated 
to them, Ministry of Development of North Eastern R egion coordinates with various 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India and S tate Governments for various development 
and welfare programmes/schemes/activities in North Eastern Region.   
 
NITI Ayog and Changes in Making Allocations 
 
1.3.5 After the constitution of the NITI Aayog, fun ds for plan as well as for non-plan schemes 
are directly allocated by Ministry of Finance in co nsultation with the concerned Ministries. The 
Ministry of Finance has decided to do away with the  distinction of funds between plan and non-
plan categories . Earlier, funds under plan schemes were allocated by the then Planning 
Commission in consultation with the concerned Minis tries. However, in the new dispensation, 
there could be discussions between NITI Aayog (to g ive a macro economic picture), Ministry of 
Finance and Ministry of DoNER before the budget is finalised. 
   
Merging of two schemes into Capacity Building & Publicity 
 
1.3.6  The schemes Advocacy & Publicity and Capacity Build ing & Technical Assistance have 
been merged with the new name Capacity Building & P ublicity by the Ministry of Finance.  
According to the Ministry, the merger of the Two He ads Advertising & Publicity and Technical 

Assistance & Capacity Building into a single head of Capacity Building and Publicity would bring 
greater synergy and facilitate in better monitoring  and evaluation of the scheme by the Ministry 
and targeting the beneficiaries better.

2.6 AGRI-HORTI POTENTIAL IN NER 
2.6.1 The Committee wanted to know in detail the co nstraints, possibilities and prospects of 
agro-horti potentials under the broad umbrella of a gricultural sector in NE region. In response the 
Ministry informed the Committee about the  issues/p roblems under agriculture and allied sector in 
the NER. 
 
Constraints to Agricultural Growth 
i. In the plain areas, small landholdings (0.63 acre p er operational holding in Assam) of the 
region preclude mechanization of agriculture.  
ii. In high altitudes, water run-off is rapid, and ther efore the region lacks water for agriculture 
during the winter season despite having abundant ra infall in summer. Therefore, lack of 
irrigation facilities and absence of water-retentio n practices severely limit possibilities of 
multiple cropping resulting in low land productivity.  
iii. Further, if rainfall turns out to be scanty, then w ater too becomes a key issue in shifting to 
the cultivation of HYVs. 
iv. In the hill, agricultural productivity is constrained not only by the paucity of water but also 
by the fact that land is held not by individuals but by the community as a whole.  
v. Lack of individual ownership rights may be an impor tant reason for the popularity of jhum 
cultivation in the hills.  
vi. The soil in hill areas is highly acidic and to neut ralize it, hill tribes often take recourse to 
burning wood and leaves to increase its alkalinity.  
vii. Further, as land is common property, cultivators ha ve no incentive to invest in it to 
improve its quality.  
 
Crop cultivation: 
i. The diverse geo-climatic conditions in the northeas t make it an ideal location for the 
cultivation of a variety of agricultural crops. Agr icultural systems remain predominantly 
traditional. The land to person ratio for the NE re gion (0.68 ha/person) is much higher than 

the national average (0.32 ha/person), with Arunach al Pradesh having the highest ratio 
(8.63 ha/person) and Assam the lowest (0.29 ha/person).  
ii. This pattern of agriculture growth has remained une ven across regions and crops. NER 
continues to be an importer of food grain as despit e covering 8.8 per cent of the country’s 
total geographical area and produces only 1.5 per c ent of the country’s total food grain 
production.  
iii. The Dependency Indices indicate that NER is highly dependent on imports for almost all 
the commodities, the only exception being spices. C ardamom, black pepper, chilli, 
turmeric and cinnamon, considered to be ‘high-value , low-volume, long –shelf-life’ 
products should be patronized. 
 
Horticulture: 
i. NER, particularly the hill areas, has tremendous pot ential for development of horticulture 
as a major contributor to the region’s economic pro sperity. It has to lead the process of 
diversification of agriculture.  
ii. In view of the climatic and altitudinal advantage a nd the tradition  of fruits and vegetable 
cultivation among the people it should not be a dif ficult goal to achieve provided a State 
specific package programme with emphasis on selected fruits  is taken up.  
iii. The programme should, among other things, provide f or needed inputs, nursery for 
planting material, processing facilities and marketing network. 
iv. The creation of marketing infrastructure has to be an important component for the 
perspective plan as markets provide the cardinal li nks so essential for agro-horticulture 
development.  
v. A modern marketing system for horticulture products is almost non-existent in North East.  
vi. A system that covers post-harvest handling, assembl y, storage, transport packing, 
processing and credit is difficult to establish given the numerous constraints.  
 
Animal Husbandry: 
i. Animal Husbandry is an important economic activity particularly in the hill areas.  
ii. Almost all the people in NER being non-vegetarian t here exists a vast market for meat and 
eggs. However, production falls a short of demand l eading to outflow of huge money on 
import from outside.  

iii. It is evident that the region is deficient by nearl y 50 per cent in milk an over 87 per cent 
eggs.  
 
Fishery: 
i. Fishery sector occupies a unique place in the socio -economic life of the people of NER, it 
being an income and employment generating activity at the primary level.  
ii. At the same time, in terms of water area and climat e, the region has tremendous potential 
for growth of pisciculture.  
iii. The freshwater species in the region are about 274 which constitute about 34 per cent of 
the country’s total stock. Assam and Tripura produce the bulk of fish.  
iv. The present per capita consumption of fish is aroun d 11 kg against the desired 
consumption level of 31 kg as recommended by the Nu trition Advisory Committee on 
Human Nutrition.  
v. On this basis the region is deficient by 55 per cen t of fish requirements which is met be 
procuring fish from outside the region at a huge cost of about Rs. 16,000 crores per annum. 
 
Sericulture: 
i. Since the North Eastern Region’s agro-climatic cond itions are most suitable for 
development of sericulture, it can be developed int o a major income earning and 
employment generating sector.  
ii. North East’s contribution towards the country’s tot al production of raw silk is generally 
about 6 per cent.  
iii. However, its contribution in terms of Muga and Seri production is more than 90 percent.  
iv. Over 3.8 lakh families are engaged in sericulture f arming and annual production recorded 
is 1063 MT.  
 
Bamboo-Based Activity: 
i. Bamboo plays an important part in the lives of the people of the NE States. It is an integral 
part of the socio-cultural and economic traditions of the region. Bamboo grows in natural 
forests, and is cultivated in homesteads, groves an d on private plantations. More than 60 
per cent of country’s bamboo resources are availabl e in the NE States and 20 per cent of 
the world’s resources are grown in the region. 

ii. At present, the volume of bamboo production falls s hort of national demand. The current 
demand for bamboo in India is estimated at 28 milli on tones, only half of which is 
presently available. So there is a need to improve the productivity of bamboo in the NE 
States, since more than 60 per cent of the bamboo resources are available here.  
iii. A number of initiatives have been taken by the Nati onal Mission on Bamboo Application 
(NMBA) to develop the bamboo sector in NER. Provisi ons have been made to arrange 
finance for bamboo development from the Technology Information Forecasting & 
Assessment Council (TIFAC), the National Mission on  Bamboo Applications, NEC, 
NEDFi and other banks.  
 
Major constraints in Agro-processing industry in the NER: 
i. Virtually no effective processing industry. 
ii. Suffering from both supply and demand problems, agr o-processing industries are grossly 
underutilized and incur losses. 
iii. Geographical isolation involving high transport costs on materials and final product. 
iv. Inadequate working capital. 
v. Poor marketing strategies with an absence of marketing networks. 
vi. Lack of market intelligence, absence of sales promotion and  
vii. Inability to compete with established brand names d ue to comparatively lower and 
uncertain quality. 
 
Certain Gaps Identified in Coffee Development in NER: 
The coffee development programme has been taken up in a scattered manner across all States of 
NER. Some gaps identified are: 
i. There is lack of adequate technical manpower to take up development activities. 
ii. Lack of involvement by concerned State agencies. 
iii. Inadequate adoption of technology by growers due to socio-economic reasons. 
iv. Poor accessibility and security issues. 
v. Long gestation period of coffee requiring sustained  investments and involvement which is 
a deterrent to tribal growers. 
vi. Only Coffee Board’s support (Rs 15,000/ha) remains insufficient to attract growers for 
consolidation activity. 

vii. Inclement weather coinciding with harvest contributing to the deterioration of quality. 
viii. Inadequate processing and marketing facilities. 
ix. Diseases/disorders specific to NER (black bean). 
 
Major Constraints for Rubber Development in NER: 
i. There are operational difficulties due to insufficient manpower 
ii. There is insufficient supply of planting material, remoteness of planting locations and poor 
communication facilities. 
iii. There has been extension to staff reduction over the last 10 years.  
iv. Frequent eruption of socio-political disturbances and militancy are other constrains. 
 
Climate: 
i. NER’s climatic conditions offer vast scope for promoting production of spices, particularly 
high value organic spices. Spices the lakadong turm eric, bird eye chilli and ginger grown 
in NER have high intrinsic value and hold vast industrial and pharmaceutical potential.  
ii. There is great scope in promoting production of org anic spices in these States by 
popularizing organic farming practices among grower s. Various schemes are being 
implemented by the Spice Board in NE States. 
 
Major Problems in Spices production include: 
i. Lack of active support from the State horti/agri departments 
ii. Non-availability of quality planting materials 
iii. Inadequate knowledge on better post-harvest practices 
iv. Lack of adequate infrastructure for quality testing, packing and storage 
v. Non-availability of organic certification facilities 
 
Land use: 
i. Forest resources generally represent over 50% of th e land area. Overall, 42% is classified 
as dense forest and 58% as open forest. Around 33% of the land area is under jhum 
cultivation, of which 18% is under current jhum. Fo rest cover has declined dramatically 
over the years.  

ii. The majority of forest land is in community ownersh ip or under the control of the 
autonomous district councils. Women and marginalize d groups have a higher dependency 
on forest resources and there is need to target the m in awareness raising, improving skills 
and promoting better livelihood technologies in forestry activities. 
 
Land tenure: 
i. Land within the NER is in the customary ownership o f the communities and clans with a 
variety of arrangement among the different tribal g roups for the allocation of different 
types of land to clan members by Chiefs, village headman, village councils, etc.  
ii. The emergence of private rights over land has contr ibuted to the concentration of land, 
particularly the better land, in the hands of a few  affluent persons within the community 
disturbing the former egalitarian character of tribal society.  
 
Farming systems:   
i. Farming systems comprise a mix of jhum (shifting) c ultivation on the hill slopes and 
settled cultivation on terraces on the lower slopes  and on the narrow valley bottoms and 
flood plains. The cropping pattern on jhum land rep resents a complex mix of intercrops 
with broadcast upland rice the dominant crop accoun ting for 70-85% of the planted area. 
Yields from the jhum are very low.  
ii. Settled agriculture on terraces and valley land is dominated by rice cultivation. Technology 
is backward with limited use of HYV and fertilizer and yields are low at 1.2-1.5 mt/ha.  
 
Credit: 
i. The virtual lack of credit facilities in NER has re presented a major constraint to the 
promotion of development activities. As a result of  the inadequacies of the formal credit 
system, communities remain dependent on informal so urces of credit, obtained from 
relatives/friends and traders/money-lenders, for bo th consumption and productive 
purposes. Interest rates are very high.  
ii. A number of significant changes have taken place in  the credit scene in the past year. 
Whilst the formal credit system remains largely unr esponsive, self-managed savings and 
credit self-help groups (SHGs) which are becoming p revalent in the rest of the India have 
begun to emerge in the NER, promoted by various NGOs.  

 
 
Priorities & thrust Areas in Agriculture 
i. A state and region specific land use policy suitabl e to different States of the region: the 
Agro-climatic Zonal planning for agriculture sector  prepared by the planning Commission 
may be considered for adoption. 
ii. Efficient extension service: The extension service that is available at present is one of the 
weakest links in agriculture development programme.  The Green Revolution made little 
impact in the North East due to a number of factors , the chief one being lack of proper 
extension network. The farmers remain uninformed ab out new methods and new 
technologies. 
iii. Institutions of appropriate level for agricultural education in all the States to train local 
farmers in knowledge and livelihood. 
iv. A workable policy for improvement of shifting culti vation through material and 
technological input support to ensure optical utili zation of Jhum lands. Such a policy to be 
evolved in consultation with the farming community. 
v. Dairying as an option to on-land farming and better animal healthcare services. 
vi. Intensive as well as extensive development of pisci-culture on scientific basis. 
vii. Make region marginally surplus in food production b y introducing integrated modern 
agricultural methods and developing agriculture horizontally and vertically 
viii. Land reforms must be undertaken 
ix. Promote horticulture on massive scale and increase area under horticulture 
x. Create efficient market infrastructure through a regional master plan 
xi. Use self-help groups as tools of change in the sector 
xii. Raised production of meat, milk and eggs.  
 
2.6.2 The Committee fully agrees with constraints  outlined by the Ministry in the above

3.1 NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES FOR NER 
 
3.1.1 In October 1996, the then Prime Minister anno unced “New Initiatives for North Eastern 
Region” and stipulated that at least 10% of the Bud get(s) of the Central Ministries/Department 
will be earmarked for the development of North East ern States. A proposal was mooted by the 
Planning Commission to the Cabinet for constitution  of such a Central Pool of Resources. The 
Cabinet approved the approach, in principle, on 15th December, 1997.  
 
3.1.2 The Prime Minister convened a Meeting of the Chief Ministers of the North Eastern States 
on 8th May 1998 when, inter alia, it was indicated that a Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources 
for the funding of specific projects in these State s would be created. The relevant paragraph from 
the Prime Minister’s speech reads as under:  
 
“We are examining the feasibility of creating a Cen tral Pool of Resources 
(CPR) which, in turn, will give critical additional  support for an 
accelerated implementation of projects in the entir e region. This pool, 
created from the unspent balance of the allocated e xpenditure of 10% of 
the budgets of the concerned Central Ministries, co uld well amount to 
around Rs.1500 crore annually.”         
   
3.1.3 This commitment of the Government was also re flected in the Speech of the Finance 
Minister while presenting the Union Budget for the year, 1998-99. The relevant paragraphs from 
the Budget Speech reads “Furthermore, it has been decided that a non-lapsab le Central 
Resources Pool will be created for deposit of funds  from all Ministries where the plan expenditure 
on the North Eastern Region is less than 10 per cen t of the total plan allocation of the Ministry. 
The difference between 10 per cent of the allocatio n and the actual expenditure incurred on the 
North Eastern Region will be transferred to the Cen tral Pool, which will be used for funding 
specific programmes for economic and social upliftment of the North Eastern States .”

ministries namely Ministry of Agriculture and Farme rs Welfare, Ministry of Road 
Transport and Ministry of Rural Development are run ning their programmes independent 
of MoDONER. The very purpose of creating the MoDONE R was that it will be a nodal 
ministry and it will coordinate with all the remain ing ministries, except the exempted 
ministries, for development of the region. This is bound to create duplication of work and it 
has been seen in the road sector. Further the trend  also has to be arrested otherwise in a

feels that the MoDONER needs to be restructured for  better coordination and 
understanding. The Committee is of the considered v iew that the role and duties of the 
MoDONER vis-à-vis other ministries has to be define d in clear terms and hence recommend 
for adequate changes in the Allocation of Business Rules, Govt. of India.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
The Committee examined the figures of national soci o-economic development 
parameters vis-a-vis socio-economic development and  growth comprising details of 
indicators like health, education, poverty, income,  unemployment, population etc in respect 
of the North Eastern States and found that health i ndicators in respect of a few states viz 
Assam and Meghalaya are very dismal. The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)  in these two states 
is higher than the national average and most shocki ng is the fact that no data is available on 
account of Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) in North E astern States except Assam which 
records very high MMR, almost double of the national average. The Committee understands 
that high IMR and high MMR reflect extremely poor a vailability of health facilities in the 
area and therefore strongly recommends  that the Mi nistry must procure MMR data in 
respect of other North Eastern states and make all out efforts to improve the situation on the 
ground in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. 
(Para 2.1.5 ) 
 
 
TOTAL REVENUE AND CAPITAL OUTLAY 
 
  The Committee was unconvinced by the  explanation o f the Ministry for allocation of 
Rs. 170 crore under SIDF over and above the budgeta ry allocation given by the Ministry for 
the simple reason that if the MoDONER was responsib le for monitoring of the projects 
under SIDF, it would have been logical to include t he allocation in the main budget 
allocation of the Ministry itself. Secondly, it is difficult to apprehend the fact that out of Rs. 
500 crore allotted in 2008-09, still Rs. 170 crore is unspent and as per the Secretary’s 
admission the Ministry has not been able to spend t he money during 2015-16 too, and if 
unspent, the money goes back to the Public Accounts . The Committee finds the allocation 
under SIDF a classic example of adhocism in budgeti ng and the role of the Ministry in 
dealing with this fund very casual. Therefore, the  Committee strongly  recommends to use 
this money on pending projects or committed liabili ties particularly when the Ministry has 
not been able to grant funds as per the projected d emands and also rationalize the allocation 
under SIDF in the next budget allocation.  
  (Para 2.2.6) 
 
 The Committee found that the Ministry had asked for  around Rs. 3850 crore as 
grants but was given only Rs. 2400 crore and this d eduction was done because the Ministry 
could not spend the money allotted in the last fina ncial year. The Committee is also given to 
understand that there is a change in the method of fund allocation to the ministries. Now the 
budget allocation is done on realistic expenditure and not on the notional expenditure. 
However, the case with the NER is different from ot her ministries, as Utilisation Certificates 
(UCs), one of the most important criteria for furth er release of grants, remain pending with 
the NE states. As per the admission of the Secretar y, DoNER, and also mentioned in the 
Outcome Budget, UCs worth Rs. 961 crore are pending . This means delay in submission of 
the UCs is affecting the budget allocation and in t urn, it is hampering the growth and 
development in the NER. The Committee in its 186 
th  Report on the Demands for Grants 
(2015-16) had suggested that the MoDONER in consult ation with North Eastern States, 
NITI Aayog and Ministry of Finance may explore a di fferent mechanism like considering a 

different time period (when there was normal weathe r in NER) for assessment of utilization 
of funds and consequent increase/decrease in alloca tion at RE stage. The Committee had 
also advised that the Ministry must continually exh ort states to ensure timely submission of 
UC/requisite documents for timely release of funds for the projects. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendations on the issue of UCs given in the 186 th  Report.

unspent money is not available to the MoDONER, the entire purpose of creating the Non-
lapsable Central Pool Resources by the Parliament will be defeated and hence recommend to 
the Ministry of DONER as well as the Ministry of Fi nance to work out a mechanism to keep
